nodes.claim: The perfect database is designed around the join, not the store: the cross-axis connection is its unit of design.
nodes.detail: The owner's purpose frame (charter §1) makes every axiom's output either powerful data in itself or a strengthener of another axiom's data — so the storage layer's success metric is the cost and expressiveness of axis-crossing reads, not write throughput or raw capacity. Schema, layout, indexing and precomputation are chosen so that the app's core operation — crossing one axis against another — is the cheapest thing the system does. A design that optimizes single-axis reads first has optimized the part of the product that is not the point.

nodes.claim: Custody is a layout property before it is a policy: the perfect database physically separates custody classes, so a policy error cannot read what the layout never co-located.
nodes.detail: World-readable aggregates, owner-readable records and device-only source data live in physically distinct stores with distinct access machinery, and the private-to-public path is a one-way fold. In such a layout a rules bug leaks nothing the layout did not already co-locate — protection by construction rather than by configuration. The genetic theory's custody-minimal claim (gen-2) is this principle applied to one axis; here it is the general storage law. Raised to cited 2026-08-28: the principle is shipped practice in clinical research infrastructure, which faces exactly this custody problem at scale. i2b2 (Murphy et al. 2010) builds identity separation into the architecture itself — a distinct Identity Management cell apart from the Data Repository cell, an honest-broker workflow, and configurable obfuscation of result counts — the obfuscation strategy is its own paper, Murphy et al. 2011 [2010 paper abstract-grade; cell architecture practice-grade from the i2b2 community wiki]. The All of Us program holds one corpus as separately versioned, separately gated materializations at different privacy depths — the Registered and Controlled tier CDRs are distinct published artifacts (v7: R2022Q4R9 and C2022Q4R9, separate data dictionaries), differing in date shifting and demographic suppression, so custody is WHICH ARTIFACT you may hold, not which row a rule lets you query [practice/repo-grade: program documentation and data dictionaries; program description in NEJM 2019, abstract-grade]. MIMIC-IV applies an irreversible per-person date shift before anything leaves the source — the custody transition is a lossy transform at a physical boundary, not a permission [abstract-grade; the shift-window figure is snippet-grade]. Product note (docs/data-inventory.md, read this run): the shipped app states the principle in one line at the push-token move — 'a field guarded by a rule is one edit from being readable, a path with no read grant is not' — and its localStorage-only rows (lens results, feed passes and deferrals, per-item timings) are device custody as layout. Environment caveat: publisher pages egress-blocked from this container; sources corroborated at two or more independent index records, grades labeled inline.

nodes.claim: The perfect database is two databases and a bridge: an append-only private ledger of events folding deterministically into exactly-shaped public read models, with the bridge as the single place custody transitions happen — and the fold's determinism is a designed property, holding only where its algebra is commutative or arrival order is retained.
nodes.detail: Restated and raised 2026-08-28 — the scout run showed the original form ('auditable, replayable, erasable per person' as free properties) understated what each costs, and the adversarial pass then moved the erasure clauses wholly into db-7, which refines this node and carries their evidence. The pedigree and the formal basis: Kreps's state-machine-replication principle — identical deterministic processes given the same inputs in the same order end in the same state — is the formal license for the fold [practice-grade]; Young's event-store formulation ('mathematically equivalent to store the end of the equation or the equation that represents it') and Kleppmann's log-centric architecture (jobs consume the log and build cached views; rebuild by re-consuming) state the two halves, and Kleppmann himself names complete deletion 'surprisingly hard' [Young full-text via a faithful repo reproduction; Kleppmann snippet-grade]. Helland grounds immutability as the distributed-coordination primitive [abstract-grade]. The fold is not free-form: self-maintainable views exist only under tight conditions (the conditions results are Quass, Gupta, Mumick & Widom 1996 and kin; surveyed in Gupta & Mumick 1995), so 'exactly-shaped' is load-bearing — shapes are chosen so the fold needs only the view and the incoming event; DBSP (VLDB 2023, Best Research Paper — award verified across three records) proves automatic incrementalization for full SQL with retraction first-class (Z-sets, negative multiplicities), which is the algebra that lets an erasure propagate into every read model; and differential dataflow (McSherry et al. 2013 — full text; the consolidation passage re-extracted verbatim from the paper's PDF this run: reconstruction cost 'will grow without bound as t increases', updates behind a frontier 'consolidated into the equivalent of a checkpoint', a step the Naiad prototype includes) shows even the ideal incremental system must compact, with the trace-compaction machinery developed further in Shared Arrangements (PVLDB 2020) [abstract-grade]. So the perfect ledger carries a compaction frontier, and the erasure boundary should be that same mechanism rather than a second, contradictory one — subject to db-7's condition that the erasure marker outlive every consumer's rebuild horizon. Two honest limits carried in-node: (1) Fowler's own caveat — read/write splitting is 'risky complexity' for most systems and is orthogonal to event sourcing — so the bundle must earn itself per reader, which db-4's frontier evidence is [snippet-grade]; (2) fold determinism holds only while the fold is commutative or arrival order is retained: the shipped replay (functions/src/replay.ts, code-verified this run) rebuilds every aggregate from append-only per-person answer docs, is exact for rank folds and unsaturated vote folds, but on a dimension at BREAKDOWN_MAX_BUCKETS eviction makes the fold order-dependent — replay yields A correct fold, not THE fold — and the edits matrix is a projection whose source deltas are not retained, so it is carried forward as its own primary fact. A projection is rebuildable, or it is primary; the design must say which, per read model. Erasure's crossing of the bridge is db-7's subject. Environment caveat: most sources corroborated at index/snippet level (egress-blocked container), grades labeled; differential dataflow read at full text.

nodes.claim: Three readers, three materializations of one ledger — layouts, not systems: no single physical layout is known to serve the device, the population fit and the research export without a measured throughput-and-freshness cost, one system over several derived shapes is the norm, the export differs by transformation and provenance rather than by scan shape, and the count of shapes grows.
nodes.detail: Raised from conjecture 2026-08-28 by the survey the seed asked for; the claim is restated to what the evidence supports, in three parts. (1) LAYOUTS, NOT SYSTEMS. The row/column divide is architectural, not schema-deep: a row store cannot capture the columnar advantage without changing both storage layer and executor (Abadi, Madden & Hachem 2008), the line of argument opened by Stonebraker & Çetintemel 2005 and C-Store 2005. And the pair-based HTAP taxonomies classify single SYSTEMS by which PAIR of shapes they maintain (Li & Zhang 2022: four classes, all pairs; Zhang et al. 2024's four storage architectures likewise), while production systems say so plainly: TiDB materializes a columnar replica (TiFlash) from its Raft log; F1 Lightning derives analytical storage from change-data-capture; Oracle's dual-format design keeps the in-memory columnar copy maintained simultaneously, with transactional consistency, against the persisted row-major format; SAP HANA — titled against the column-store myth — still runs per-lifecycle-stage formats (delta row, read-optimized main). One interface, several shapes, is the industry's converged answer. (2) 'CANNOT' WEAKENS TO A MEASURED FRONTIER. Monolithic single-format HTAP exists as a named survey category (Song et al. 2024, facing 'contradictory format demands'), and HyPer served both workloads from one representation plus fork/copy-on-write snapshots at claimed best-of-breed [abstract-grade — though the snapshot is itself a transient second materialization]; Milkai et al. 2022 formalize the real cost as a measurable throughput frontier plus a freshness-versus-isolation trade. So the claim is about cost, not possibility. (3) THE EXPORT IS A DIFFERENT AXIS, AND THE COUNT GROWS. What makes a research export its own materialization is irreversible transformation, freezing, versioning and provenance — MIMIC-IV's per-person date shift, All of Us's tiered CDRs, the FAIR artifact properties — not scan efficiency; Chorus shows interactive privacy can be a query rewrite over the production store, so the export's separateness rests on citability and lossy de-identification, which a rewrite cannot give. And feature-store practice already runs row + column + vector behind one API (Hopsworks 2024; the embedding shift, Orr et al. 2021), so three is today's count, not a law. Prior art and rival, named: OctopusDB (CIDR 2011, vision track) is this exact architecture — storage views in different physical layouts over a logical event log as primary storage — proposed and never productized; BigDAWG answers the same no-one-size premise with federation over heterogeneous engines instead. The ledger-derivation answer fits this system better because its honesty contract requires every published number recomputable (pat-2), which federation does not give. Environment caveat: publisher pages egress-blocked; all sources corroborated at two or more independent index records; C-Store's famous speedup figures are snippet-grade and deliberately not quoted in the claim.

nodes.claim: Schema evolution is a first-class operation: every change is a named, ordered version whose transition commits all-or-none and never lands half-applied, while the data rewrite behind it may be eager, lazy or incremental along a measured latency-versus-migration-cost frontier — and every prior shape stays readable, by reader/writer resolution or by intermediate states, until the last consumer has moved off it.
nodes.detail: Raised to cited 2026-09-02, claim restated: the literature treats schema change as a versioned protocol and is unanimous that old shapes stay readable while consumers move — but it does NOT support eager all-at-once data rewrite, so all-or-none now binds the version transition, not the rewrite. Schemas do not stop changing: Curino, Moon, Tanca & Zaniolo's Wikipedia study reports 170+ schema versions over 4.5 years, 41.5% of original attributes removed and 25.1% renamed [snippet-grade]; Qiu, Li & Su, over 160K revisions of ten open-source database applications, find schemas evolve frequently and schema changes induce significant code-level modification [abstract-grade]. Rae et al.'s F1 protocol is the mechanism: a change decomposes into intermediate delete-only and write-only states, safe 'so long as all servers are no more than one schema version behind at any time' [abstract-grade], a lease keeping at most two versions live [repo-grade: CockroachDB RFC]. That is the precise shape of all-or-none — each transition commits atomically, but a sequence of safe steps carries the system across, never one global flip. Readability of old shapes is the reader/writer split: Avro resolves a writer's schema against a reader's and signals an error only where a reader field has no default [repo-grade]; Confluent's registry makes the survival condition mechanical — BACKWARD demands consumers upgrade first, FULL lets either side move [practice-grade]; Herrmann et al. push co-existing schema versions into the database itself [abstract-grade]; Kleppmann: data outlives code, so compatibility is needed in both directions [practice-grade]; Ambler & Sadalage's transition period keeps both shapes until dependent teams move, 'several quarters, if not years' [snippet-grade]. The correction: Störl, Klettke, Hillenbrand et al. show eager rewrite buys latency at a price in billed reads and writes, lazy is cheaper but pays on access and accumulates chains of pending operations on entities written releases ago — the longitudinal failure mode, so a long-lived personal store must cap that chain [abstract-grade]. Product note (docs read this run): the shipped app's compatibility trap is the sharper lesson — a defaulted getter treating an absent field as a value read as the backward-compatible shape and leaked in queries; what shipped was a required boolean (D65). A read-time default is a claim about old data its writer never made: a default is itself a migration and must be versioned like one.

nodes.claim: The join's currency is sufficient statistics carrying their basis, not raw rows — but sufficiency is relative to the join's estimand: each cross-axis quantity is a statistic sufficient for the joint target, computed jointly over the sources — within a person by their own custody, across custodians by secure computation, never by physically pooling two custody classes (marginal per-axis summaries do not identify cross-axis structure), naming its n, provenance, reference basis and version so composition is arithmetically valid, and cleared through disclosure control because a derived quantity is not automatically custody-preserving; under those conditions the join is custody-preserving and recomputable at once.
nodes.detail: Raised to cited 2026-09-02, restated with three clauses the evidence forces. Sufficiency is why a derived quantity can stand in for rows (Fisher 1922 [snippet-grade, via secondary]; the factorization theorem, Neyman 1935 and Halmos & Savage 1949 [abstract-grade]). Built practice: DataSHIELD links site analyses by 'non-disclosive summary statistics' and reproduces individual-level GLM meta-analysis (Gaye et al. 2014) [abstract-grade]; GLORE exchanges 'partially aggregated intermediary results' and matches centralized logistic regression 'to a 10^-15 precision' (Wu et al. 2012) [snippet-grade]; OHDSI's 250-million-patient study ran queries locally and returned only aggregate results centrally (Hripcsak et al. 2016); Lin & Zeng 2010 prove no asymptotic efficiency loss under three named conditions (common parameter of interest, distinct nuisance parameters, ML-based summaries) [all abstract-grade]. Clause one, sufficiency is join-relative: fixed-size sufficient statistics exist only inside exponential families (Koopman–Pitman–Darmois) [snippet-grade]; aggregate correlations can invert individual ones (Robinson 1950; Berlin et al. 2002) — so the cross-axis term is computed jointly and never recomposed from marginals — and where the sources sit under different custody the vertical-partition protocols recover the exact joint regression by secure matrix product across custodians holding disjoint attributes of the same persons (Sanil et al. 2004; Karr et al. 2009) [abstract-grade]. Clause two, the basis travels: unaccounted subject overlap 'can greatly inflate type I error' (Lin & Sullivan 2009) [abstract-grade]; summary GWAS statistics read only against a declared reference (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015; Pasaniuc & Price 2017), and GWAS-SSF pairs every statistics file with mandatory metadata [practice-grade]. Clause three, derived is not safe: allele frequencies re-identify contributors (Homer et al. 2008), shared gradients invert to training data (Zhu et al. 2019), and too many accurate aggregates reconstruct the database under any disclosure method (Dinur & Nissim 2003; Dwork & Roth 2014) [abstract-grade] — so publication passes disclosure control (Hundepool et al. 2012) or secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al. 2017) first. Latent axes travel as plausible values (Mislevy 1991; von Davier et al. 2009). The currency costs: summary-statistic imputation recovers 84%/54% of effective sample size against 89%/67% from genotypes (Pasaniuc et al. 2014) [abstract-grade]. Product note: the shipped app joins in clause one's shape — anchors frozen onto each answer at write, in the person's partition, so the fold publishes joint question×anchor cells with counts rather than recomposing them later — though one anchor dimension at a time (foldAnchors keys dim→bucket→option, so anchor×anchor structure is exactly the marginal not identified); what D98's exact publication costs under the reconstruction law, this graph does not yet carry.

nodes.claim: Per-person erasure is a transaction across ledger, bridge and read models — and key destruction counts as erasure only conditionally: the honest design keeps personal payloads out of the immutable structure so erasure is ordinary deletion, scopes crypto-shredding to backups and immutable media under verifiably irreversible key destruction, records each erasure as a permanent fact, and lets only anonymous folds survive.
nodes.detail: Added 2026-08-28. The write side's canonical answer to deletion was a compensating event (Young, db-3), which is exactly what erasure law does not accept: the GDPR's structural premise is mutability (Finck, EP STOA study 2019), and regulators treat key destruction as erasure only conditionally, never simpliciter — the EDPB's blockchain guidelines (02/2025, v2.0 adopted 2026-07-07; found by this run's adversarial pass after the scout missed them) accept fulfilment of the right to erasure by destruction of a securely managed off-chain decryption key, or deletion of the off-chain component, where on-chain storage is unavoidable; CNIL 2018 holds on-chain erasure 'technically impossible' and says the cryptographic workarounds 'do not, strictly speaking, result in an erasure of the data' while blessing deletion of off-chain-referenced data; the ICO's beyond-use doctrine permits treating undeletable backup data as deleted under four conditions, one of which is permanent deletion as soon as it becomes possible; and the EDPB's coordinated erasure enforcement report (adopted 2026-02-18) names backups and weak anonymisation-as-substitute as the enforcement failure zones [all snippet-grade via multiple independent legal-press and regulator index records]. The reconciliation is layered and each layer is named. (1) FORGETTABLE PAYLOADS, the primary mechanism: personal data lives outside the immutable structure and is referenced from it; erasure is ordinary deletion in a mutable store; the ledger keeps its shape and order, and the fold must treat an absent payload as a first-class case (Verraes 2019 — the shape CNIL independently blesses off-chain). (2) CRYPTO-SHREDDING, scoped to immutable media and backups — the one place key destruction genuinely beats deletion, and exactly where the EDPB found controllers failing — grounded in NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2's cryptographic erase with its stated prerequisites: no plaintext ever on the medium, verifiable key zeroization [snippet-grade; Rev. 1 was withdrawn 2025-09-26 — cite Rev. 2]. CJEU C-413/23 P's relative-identifiability holding (2025-09-04) helps this leg only if key destruction is architecturally irreversible from the controller's own position [snippet-grade, nine legal-press records]. (3) EXCISION as the escape hatch, with Datomic's refinement: the erasure itself leaves a permanent record — auditability of the FACT of erasure is a different, achievable property than auditability of the erased content, and it is what keeps db-3's 'auditable' true through an erasure rather than in spite of it [practice-grade, vendor docs]. The failure modes are mechanical, not philosophical: crypto-shredding does not reach derived read models computed from plaintext — the read side is where erasure actually fails, per the pattern's own advocate's caveat (Verraes) — so erasure must propagate through the bridge into every read model (DBSP's first-class retractions are the algebra for this, db-3); and log-compaction tombstones expire (Kafka delete.retention.ms, default one day; Apache JIRA KAFKA-7137), after which a rebuild reconstructs the erased person — replayability and erasure conflict at mechanism level unless the erasure marker outlives every consumer's rebuild horizon [practice-grade]. Product note (code and docs read this run): the shipped app is a fourth technique in miniature — person-partitioned sources (per-uid answer docs; deleteAccount erases by partition sweep), a uid-bearing ledger that TTLs at 90 days, anonymous folds surviving deletion, and D293 recording the honest residual (moderation-verdict rows whose ids carry uids). Environment caveat: legal and standards documents were unreachable from this container; every source corroborated at two or more independent index or legal-press records, grades labeled; the peer-reviewed treatment of this tension lives in the blockchain-immutability literature (Politou et al. 2019), not in an event-sourcing literature, which does not exist at peer-reviewed grade.

nodes.claim: The read side's publishable grain is bounded by the answer-density budget and the serving policy, not by storage: the daily observation budget is conserved — population times a small, effort-bounded number of answers per person-day — however large the bank grows, so adding questions divides a fixed budget; and because a serving policy makes who answers a question policy-selected, an aggregate is a population claim only if its read model carries its sampling design: the serving and response propensities recorded at serve time, or covariates rich enough to render the selection ignorable.
nodes.detail: Raised to cited 2026-09-02, restated with the 'or' the evidence forces. DENSITY. The 2012 Xbox opt-in poll ran this shape — a bank under a per-person daily cap: 'Each day, three to five questions were posted', 'respondents were allowed to answer at most once per day', 750,148 interviews from 345,858 respondents (Wang, Rothschild, Goel & Gelman 2015) [full text]. EMA studies average six assessments a day at 79% compliance across 496 samples (Wrzus & Neubauer 2023) [snippet-grade]; longer questionnaires raised burden and degraded data while three-to-nine prompts a day alone did not (Eisele et al. 2022) [abstract-grade] — the budget is denominated in items and effort, not prompts. SERVING POLICY AS MEANING. Selection, not size, governs error: a self-selected 1% of US voters carries the error of a random sample near 400 once the data-defect correlation is priced (Meng 2018) [abstract-grade, paraphrase]; Delphi–Facebook's quarter-million weekly responses overstated vaccine uptake by 17 points (Bradley et al. 2021) [abstract-grade]. The design is part of the datum operationally: replay evaluation is unbiased only for streams 'from a uniformly random logging policy', weakened to any randomized logging policy via rejection sampling at a cost in data efficiency (Li et al. 2011) [full text]; counterfactual estimates need 'active randomization', and 'each data sample needs to provide ... the values of all variables needed to evaluate the factors that do not cancel in the ratio' (Bottou et al. 2013) [full text]; hence the Open Bandit Dataset logs 'true propensity scores' per row [repo-grade]. Randomly exposed ratings differ markedly from user-selected ones, so error on user-selected items 'is clearly an unreliable estimate ... over the whole rating matrix' (Marlin & Zemel 2009) [full text]. Contrary, now in the claim: poststratification corrected the 93%-male Xbox sample from respondent covariates alone, no propensity logged (Wang et al. 2015) [full text]; Steck 2010 gets unbiased measures under MNAR by modelling the mechanism [snippet-grade]. Product note (docs read this run): the shipped app removes only the SERVING half of the selection — the Mirror folds core, served to everyone unpersonalized (D161) — and leaves response self-selection, for which its frozen anchors are the poststratification covariates Wang et al. used, not a logged propensity; it cannot take the full propensity branch: D316/D317 made the server choose what the tail offers, so serving is knowable, but the response side stays device-local (D317 keeps D163's pass/defer line unbuilt) and only sampled anonymous shards carry per-question seen/passed buckets (D271). Tail aggregates publish without a sampling design and are not population claims.

nodes.claim: Every ledger fact is bitemporal by contract: it carries the valid-time person-state snapshot in force when it was recorded — the anchors and the asking context, held as a determinate stand-in for an indeterminate reality — and a transaction time per published read model it entered (this lane's inference; the literature fixes one transaction time per database), with corrections appended rather than snapshots mutated (erasure excepted: db-7's forgettable payloads are deleted, not corrected); because each axis is lossy in one direction, this is what makes within-person joins as-of by construction and every published cross-source number reproducible wherever db-3's determinism condition holds.
nodes.detail: Added 2026-09-02, cited. The two-axis split is foundational, not this lane's: Snodgrass & Ahn (SIGMOD 1985) separated valid from transaction time [snippet-grade]; the consensus glossary fixes them — valid time 'when the fact is true in the modeled reality', transaction time 'when the fact is current in the database and may be retrieved' (Jensen et al. 1994); SQL:2011 standardized both (Kulkarni & Michels 2012) [snippet-grade]. Load-bearing is the lossiness: a rollback database views tuples 'as of that time', a historical one 'as of now', and only one carrying both — his 'temporal' class — 'can thus record retroactive changes' (Snodgrass 1990) [snippet-grade; the as-of phrases at one record only] — so a snapshot that froze a wrong anchor is repaired by a later transaction-time record, never by mutation (Fowler 2021) [practice-grade]; XTDB [repo-grade] and Datomic's as-of/history [practice-grade] ship this. The as-of join half is prior art, named as such (Kimball's Type 2 dimension, in sources); feature stores industrialize it — Feast's point-in-time join reproduces 'the state of features at a specific point in the past' and, filtered on created timestamp, 'what the online store would have served at each event time' [repo-grade]; Hopsworks (SIGMOD 2024) [snippet-grade]. Reproducing a published number pins its inputs to a transaction time: Delta Lake time travel (Armbrust et al. 2020) [snippet-grade]. The wrong axis is a named error: leakage (Kaufman et al. 2012), immortal time bias (Suissa 2008), time-varying confounding over person-period data (Robins 1986; Singer & Willett 2003) [snippet-grade]. This lane's inference over that base, marked: (1) transaction time is PER READ MODEL — one valid time, n entry times, and only the per-surface time reproduces what that surface showed (no source found either way); (2) the asking context belongs inside valid time, since answers co-vary with wording, order and mode (Tourangeau, Rips & Rasinski 2000) [snippet-grade]; (3) 'as published' and 'as best known' are two reproduction targets, and a read model says which. Limits: DBMS 'support for temporal data is still in its infancy' (Kaufmann et al. 2014); valid time is formally indeterminate (Dyreson & Snodgrass 1998) [snippet-grade]. Product note (code read this run): the shipped answer doc is the valid-time half — anchors frozen with answeredAt (D8), an edit moving only optionIdx in place (D86) — and the loadings doc's server timestamp and the graded call's published inputs snapshot are per-read-model transaction pins in miniature; but the fact itself is uni-temporal, so a pre-edit aggregate is reproducible only inside the 90-day ledger horizon.
